knowledge.title: Proverbs on speech, silence and words / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan hadalka
knowledge.text:
- Af daboolan waa dahab. – "A closed mouth is gold." Silence is often wiser than speech.
- Hadal badan haan ma buuxsho. – "Much talk does not fill a milk vessel." Talk without action achieves nothing.
- Af jooga looma adeego. – "One does not speak for a mouth that is present." Let people speak for themselves when they are there.
- Hadal intuu uurkaaga ku jiro ayuu ammaan yahay. – "A word is safe while it is still in your belly." Once said, you cannot control it; keep secrets.
- Hadal nin si u yiri, ninna si u qaaday. – "One man said it one way, another took it another way." Words are easily misunderstood.
- Hadal nin badiyey ma wada odhan, nin yareeyayna kama wada tegin. – "The one who talked a lot did not say everything; the one who talked little did not leave everything out." Being brief costs nothing.
- Qawl nin weyn ka dhacay waa qolof geed ka dhacday. – "A word dropped by an important man is like bark fallen from a tree." It cannot be put back: leaders must keep their word.
- Caano aan fiiqsi loo dhamin iyo hadal aan fiiro loo odhan feedhahaaga ayay wax yeelaan. – "Milk gulped without sipping and words spoken without thought both hurt your ribs." Think before speaking.
- Af wax cunay xishood. / Nin wax cunay xishood. – "A mouth that has eaten feels shy." People who have received favours hesitate to criticise their benefactor.
- Afxumo nabadna waa kaa geysaa, colaadna wax kaagama tarto. – "A foul tongue costs you peace and does not help you in war either."
- Aan wada hadalno waa aan heshiinno. – "'Let's talk' means 'let's make peace'." Dialogue is the road to reconciliation; often quoted in mediation.
- Dhegi meel dheer bay ku dhacdaa, dhagaxna meel dhow. – "A word travels far, a stone falls near." Words reach further than force.

knowledge.title: Proverbs on unity and cooperation / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan midnimada
knowledge.text:
- Iskaashato ma kufto. – "Those who support each other do not fall." The classic proverb of mutual help; popular for cooperatives and community projects.
- Far keliya fool ma dhaqdo. – "One finger cannot wash a face." Nobody succeeds alone.
- Ilko wada jir bay wax ku gooyaan. – "Teeth cut only when they work together." Unity is strength.
- Gacmo wada jir bay wax ku gooyaan. – "Hands cut (tear) things only together." Same meaning as the above; used for teamwork.
- Geeljire geela waa wada jiraa, waana kala jiraa. – "Camel herders are together with the herd, yet each keeps to his own camels." People cooperate but still look after their own interests.
- Ilko abeeso hoos bay ka xidhiidhaan. – "A snake's fangs are joined at the root." Kin are bound by ties that cannot be broken; relatives quarrel but stay connected.
- Gacmo is dhaafaa gacalo ka timaaddaa. – "Affection comes from hands that pass things to each other." Giving and exchanging gifts builds love.
- Laba qaawan isma qaado. – "Two naked people cannot clothe (carry) each other." Two people in the same need cannot rescue one another.
- Barti-yaqaan bari uma kororto. – "The herd of a man who knows only one pasture does not grow." Isolation and narrowness keep you poor; widen your circle.
- Fiqi tolkii kama janno tago. – "A religious scholar will not enter Paradise without his kin." Kinship ties are so strong that even the pious cannot cut loose from their relatives.
Usage: these are the safest proverbs for public messages, school talks and business pitches because they carry no negative edge. knowledge.title: Proverbs on knowledge, advice and wisdom / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan aqoonta iyo talada
knowledge.text:
- Aqoon la'aani waa iftiin la'aan. – "Lack of knowledge is lack of light." Widely used to promote education; a common school motto.
- Nin aan dhul marin dhaayo ma leh. – "He who has not travelled has no eyes." Travel and experience bring understanding. (Also recorded as "Nin aan dhul marini dhaayo la'.")
- Talo walaal diide taagoogta ayuu ka jabaa. – "One who refuses a brother's advice breaks his shin." Ignoring advice from those close to you brings harm.
- Talo xumo tog baas bay kaa riddaa. – "Bad counsel throws you into a nasty ravine."
- Talo adigaa ku nool ee iyadu kuguma noola. – "You live by advice; advice does not live by you." You need counsel more than it needs you – value it.
- Taladaan la ruugin waa lagu rafaadaa. – "A decision that is not chewed over makes you suffer." Deliberate before deciding.
- Ama talo keen ahow, ama talo raac ahow. – "Either be one who brings a plan, or one who follows a plan." Either lead with ideas or cooperate; do not just obstruct.
- Intaadan falin ka fiirso. – "Before you act, look." Equivalent of "look before you leap".
- Waano abuur baa ka horreysay. – "Nature came before advice." Advice cannot change a person's inborn character.
- Damiin faro waaweyn baa wax loogu qoraa. – "For a dull pupil one must write in big letters." Slow learners need things made very plain.
- Arrinxumo abaar ka daran. – "A bad decision is worse than a drought."
- Nin aan waxa jooga garani waxa soo socda ma garto. – "He who does not understand what is here now will not understand what is coming."

knowledge.title: Proverbs on patience, effort and work / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan dulqaadka iyo dadaalka
knowledge.text:
- Qof aan dhididin ma dhergo. – "One who does not sweat does not get full." No effort, no reward. (Recorded in some collections as "Qof aan dhididini ma dhego.")
- Nin sabraa sed leh. – "A patient man gets his share." Patience pays.
- Qun-yar-socde qodaxi ma muddo. – "A thorn does not prick the one who walks slowly." Careful, unhurried people avoid harm.
- Hadday degdegsiinyo door dhalaan, kaadsiinyana kiish lacagay dhalaan. – "If haste gives birth to a little, patience gives birth to a bag of money."
- Fadhi iyo fuud yicibeed laysku waa. – "Sitting at home and yicib-nut soup never go together." Yicib (yeheb) nuts grow in remote places; good things require going out to work.
- Biyo sacabbadaada ayaa looga dhergaa. – "You only quench your thirst with water from your own palms." Self-reliance: what you earn yourself satisfies you.
- Wadiiqada yari waddada weyn bay kugu riddaa. – "The small path leads you onto the big road." Small beginnings lead to big results.
- Intii calooshu buki lahayd cagtu ha bukto. – "Better that the foot aches than the belly (heart)." Better to tire yourself doing it now than to regret later.
- Dheri ninkii ag jooga ayaa lafta kala baxa. – "The one who sits by the cooking pot gets the bone." Be present where opportunities are.
- Dhubuq-dhubuq hore dhabanno-hays dambe ayay leedahay. – "Rushing at first ends with holding your cheeks (in regret) later."
- Gees lo'aad kulaylkaa lagu gooyaa. – "A cow's horn is cut while it is hot." Strike while the iron is hot.
- Rag waxaa u liita ma toshe, ma tashade iyo ma tashiishe. – "The worst men are the one who does not mend, does not consult and does not save." Praise for practicality, consultation and thrift.

knowledge.title: Proverbs on truth, lies and honesty / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan runta iyo beenta
knowledge.text:
- Soomaali been ma maahmaahdo. – "Somalis don't lie in proverbs." Proverbs are taken as accepted truth.
- Been fakatay runi ma gaarto. – "Truth cannot catch up with a lie that has run off." Once a lie spreads, correcting it is hard – act early.
- Beentaada hore runtaada dambe bay u baas baxdaa. – "Your earlier lie damages your later truth." (Variant: "Beentaada hore runtaada dambe ayay dishaa" – kills your later truth.) Liars lose credibility.
- Beeni raad ma leh. – "A lie leaves no footprint." A lie has no substance and leads nowhere.
- Beenaale markhaatigiisuu fogeeyaa. – "A liar places his witness far away." Liars cite sources nobody can check.
- Runi rag waa ka nixisaa, waxse ma yeesho. – "Truth may frighten a man, but it does him no harm."
- Fari qorrax ma qariso. – "A finger cannot hide the sun." The truth cannot be concealed.
- Daacadi ma hungowdo. – "Honesty never goes empty-handed." Honesty is always rewarded.
- Sirow ma hodmo. – "The cheat does not prosper."
- Ballandarro waa diindarro. – "Breaking a promise is like having no religion." Keeping one's word is a religious duty.
- Fallaadhi gilgilasho kaagama go'do. – "An arrow does not fall out of you however you shake." Once exposed, excuses do not help.
Usage: these suit fact-checking and trust contexts – e.g., an assistant gently warning about misinformation: "'Been fakatay runi ma gaarto' – war aan la hubin ha faafin" (don't spread unverified news). knowledge.title: Proverbs on caution, risk and misfortune / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan feejignaanta iyo belaayada
knowledge.text:
- Abeesadii lix jir kugu qaniintaa lixdan jir bay kugu dishaa. – "The snake that bites you at six kills you at sixty." Old harms and grudges linger a lifetime.
- Belaayo kaa sii jeedda layskuma soo jeediyo. – "Don't turn towards you a trouble that is facing away." Do not provoke trouble that is leaving you alone.
- Belaayo ka-hor-tag mooyee ka-dabo-tag ma leh. – "Misfortune can be headed off in front, never chased from behind." Prevention works; cure after the fact often doesn't.
- Belaayo intay kaa maqan tahay, qayrkaa bay ku maqan tahay. – "While misfortune is away from you, it is with your peers." Don't gloat – your turn may come.
- Bannaankiisa-mare maradiisa geed ma qabsato. – "The cloth of one who walks in the open is not caught by a tree." The cautious avoid trouble.
- Booraan hadimo ha qodin, ku dhici doontaana mooyee. – "Do not dig a trap-pit, unless you want to fall into it." Plots against others backfire.
- Biyo intaysan ku soo gaarin ayaa layska moosaa. – "Build the dyke before the water reaches you." Prepare in advance.
- Caano daatay dabadooda la qabtaa. – "When milk spills, you grab its tail." Save what you can after a loss.
- Dab aan ku gubin kulaylkiisa ma ogid. – "You don't know the heat of a fire that hasn't burned you." Only experience teaches how bad something is.
- Nin qoyani biyo iskama dhowro. – "A man already wet does not avoid water." Once deep in a situation, there's no point holding back.
- Col kaa badan iyo biyo kaa badanba way ku hafiyaan. – "An enemy larger than you and water deeper than you both drown you." Know your limits.
- Ama afeef hore lahow, ama adkaysi dambe lahow. – "Either refuse at the start or endure to the end." Don't accept a task and then quit.
- Bidaari sibiq bay kugu gashaa. – "Baldness creeps up on you unnoticed." Troubles arrive gradually and unexpectedly.

knowledge.title: Proverbs on people, character and relationships / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan dadka iyo dabeecadda
knowledge.text:
- Aadane eed ma waayo. – "A human being is never without fault." Everyone makes mistakes – forgive.
- Barasho horteed ha i nicin. – "Don't hate me before you know me." Do not judge by appearance. (Kapchits links it to a tale of an ugly but brave suitor.)
- Nin aanad saacad ku baran sannad kuma baratid. – "A man you couldn't get to know in an hour, you won't know in a year." First impressions of character are revealing.
- Baqal fardo la daaqday faras bay is mooddaa. – "A mule that grazed with horses thinks it is a horse." Company can give people airs.
- Maroodiga takarta saaran ma arkee kan kale tan saaran ayuu arkaa. – "The elephant doesn't see the fly on itself but sees the one on another elephant." People see others' faults, not their own.
- Ninkaad kabo ka tolanaysid kuwiisaa la eegaa. – "When you want a man to make you shoes, look at his own shoes." Judge skill by results.
- Nin geed geli jiray geed looma galo. – "You can't ambush a man who used to ambush from trees." You cannot trick someone with his own tricks.
- Nin tuur lihi siduu u seexdo isagaa yaqaan. – "The hunchback knows how he should sleep." People know their own needs best.
- Wax qof la toosan baa qof la tuur leh. – "What is straight to one person is crooked to another." Perspectives differ.
- La-yeele ma hilmaamo, laakiin yeele wuu hilmaamaa. – "The wronged one does not forget; the wrongdoer does."
- Mar i dage Alle ha dago, mar labaad i dagase anaa is dagay. – "If he cheats me once, may God punish him; if he cheats me twice, I cheated myself." Fool me once...
- Abaal nin gala waa la arkay, nin gudase lama arag. – "Many are seen accepting a favour; none are seen repaying it." Gratitude is rare.
- Calool dheregsani calool baahan kama naxdo. – "A full belly feels no pity for a hungry one."
- Geel laba jir soo wada mar. – "All camels were once two years old." Everyone was young and inexperienced once.
- Meel lagaa jecel yahay haddaad ka tagto, meel lagaa neceb yahay ayaad tagtaa. – "If you leave a place where you are loved, you end up where you are disliked."

knowledge.title: Proverbs on life, fate, need and generosity / Maahmaahyo ku saabsan nolosha iyo deeqsinimada
knowledge.text:
- Gar iyo geeri loo siman. – "Justice and death treat all equally." Everyone is equal before the law and mortality.
- Gari Ilaah bay taqaan. – "Justice knows (only) God." A fair verdict favours no side.
- Waari mayside war ha kaa haro. – "You won't live forever, so let a good name remain after you."
- Geed walba in gubtaa hoos taal. – "Under every tree lies something that scorches it." Everyone has hidden troubles.
- Timir laf baa ku jirta. – "There is a stone in every date." Every good thing has a flaw.
- Khayr wax kaama dhimee shar u toog hay. – "Good times cost you nothing, but stay ready for bad times." Hope for the best, prepare for the worst.
- Arrini madax la qabtay leedahaye mijo la qabto ma leh. – "A matter has a head to grab, not a heel." Tackle problems at their source.
- Kabxume ma hadhee kablaawaa hadha. – "It's not the one with bad shoes who falls behind, but the one with no shoes." Something is better than nothing.
- Miro gunti ku jira kuwo geed saaran looma daadiyo. – "Don't throw away the fruit in your waist-cloth for fruit still on the tree." A bird in the hand.
- Baahi badan, baryo badan iyo bukaan badanba waa laysku nacaa. – "Constant need, constant begging and constant illness all make people weary of you."
- Dani xishood ma leh. – "Need has no shame." People in need will ask for anything.
- Lafo geri ayagaa laysku jebiyaa. – "Giraffe bones are broken only against each other." A hard problem needs an equally strong tool.
- Cadowgaaga caano mac ayaa la siiyaa. – "Give your enemy sweet milk." Disarm hostility with hospitality.
- Dab aan kulaylkiisa la arag dambaskiisa lagama leexdo. – "If you haven't felt the fire's heat, you don't step around its ashes." You fear a person's anger only after seeing it.
- Cimrigaagoo dheeraadaa geel dhalayuu ku tusaa. – "A long life will show you a camel giving birth." Live long enough and you'll see rare things.
- Dhar magaalo intii laga xirto waa dhowdahay, dhal magaalase intii lagu noqdo waa dheer tahay. – "Town clothes are quick to put on; becoming a true townsman takes long." Real change takes time.

knowledge.title: Somali dialects overview: Northern, Benadir, Maay / Lahjadaha Af-Soomaaliga
knowledge.text:
Somali varieties fall into three main groups (Saeed 1999; Lamberti 1986):
1. Northern (Af-Maxaa, also 'Maxaa-tiri' – 'those who say maxaa' for 'what'). Spoken by more than 70% of Somalis: Somaliland, Djibouti, Puntland, central Somalia, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and north-eastern Kenya. Subgroups: Northern proper (north-west: Isaaq, Gadabuursi, Ciise, Warsangeli, Dhulbahante speech), the Darod / north-eastern group (Bari, Nugaal, Mudug, Ethiopia's Somali Region, Gedo), and the Lower Juba variety. Standard Somali (written since 1972) is based on Northern Somali, and almost all classical poetry is in it. 2. Benadir / Coastal (Af-Benaadir, Af-Reer Xamar in Mogadishu). Spoken on the Benadir coast from Hobyo to south of Marka, including Mogadishu. Largely mutually intelligible with Northern; it has some extra sounds and loanwords (including from Harari and Arabic). Subvarieties include the Abgaal/Ajuuraan/Galjecel speech and the urban Xamari of old Mogadishu. 3. Maay (Af-Maay, Maay Maay) – spoken by the Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn) clans and many Somali Bantu in the inter-riverine south (Bay, Bakool, Gedo, Lower and Middle Shabelle, Jubba areas; Baidoa/Baydhabo is the centre). Only partly intelligible to Northern speakers – often compared to Spanish vs Portuguese. Maay speakers usually also understand Standard Somali via media and school. Smaller varieties: Jiiddu, Dabarre, Tunni, Garre (Garre is close to Aweer), and Af-Ashraaf of Marka and Shingaani (old Mogadishu).
Political note: Somalia's 2004 transitional charter named Af-Maay and Af-Maxaa as official varieties; a separate Maay alphabet has been developed since the 1980s.
For an assistant (voice and text):
- Default to Standard Somali in output, but understand regional forms in input.
- Ask "Ma waxaad ku hadashaa Af-Maay?" only if the input clearly isn't Maxaa; never imply a dialect is 'broken Somali'.
- Recognisers trained on Northern speech often mistranscribe Benadiri and Maay words; normalise to standard spelling before reasoning (see the spelling-variants and Maay entries).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_dialects; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maay_language; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benadiri_Somali; Hassan, Deqa (2011). Somali Dialects in the United States: How Intelligible is Af-Maay to Speakers of Af-Maxaa? MA thesis, Minnesota State Univ. https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/etds/276/

knowledge.title: Northern (Hargeysa) vs. Southern/Benadiri (Muqdisho) differences / Kala duwanaanta Waqooyi iyo Koonfur
knowledge.text:
Standard written Somali hides much variation. Commonly noticed differences between Northern (Hargeysa, Burco, Djibouti) and Southern/Benadiri (Muqdisho) speech:
Sounds and spelling
- dh vs r: many words with dh in the North have r in the South: xidh / xir (tie, close), odhan / oran (to say), idhi / iri (I said), yidhi / yiri (he said), badh / bar (half), adhi / ari (sheep and goats). Both spellings are accepted; Northern writers favour dh.
- kh vs q / x in Arabic loans: wakhti (North) vs waqti (South) 'time'; khudaar / qudaar (vegetables).
- The past ending -ay is often pronounced/written -ey in the North (keeney, sameeyey) and -ay in the South (keenay, sameeyay).
Vocabulary and expressions
- Copula at sentence end: North "weeye" ("Nabad weeye"); South "waaye" ("Meeqa waaye?" how much is it; "Nabad waaye").
- How much: North "Waa immisa?"; South "Meeqa?" / "Meeqa waaye?".
- Who is it?: North "Waa kuma?"; South "Waa ayo?".
- Yes/OK: North "haye"; both "haa".
- Greeting: "Iska warran?" and "Maxaad sheegtay?" are heard more in the North; "Seetahay?" (Sidee tahay?) is typical of Mogadishu.
- Benadiri/Mogadishu speech uses more Italian- and Arabic-origin words in daily life (e.g., shukumaan 'towel', baasto 'pasta').
- The number laba 'two' is often pronounced and written "labo" in the South ("labo kun" 2,000).
Grammar
- The progressive suffix is -ay- in standard Somali; some dialects use -na- (Wikipedia: "-ay- / -na- depending on dialect").
- Benadiri has some extra phonemes and loanwords from Harari (Banti).
Names for the capital: Muqdisho (official), Xamar (common, esp. South), "Xamar Cad", "Xamar Weyne" (the old quarter). Hargeysa is also spelled Hargeisa in English. For transcription: accept both members of each pair (xidh/xir, wakhti/waqti, keeney/keenay) as the same word; output one consistent spelling – by default the user's own, otherwise the standard dictionary form.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_dialects; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benadiri_Somali; https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/naxwe/08-hogatuska-baradigmaha-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0)

knowledge.title: Af-Maay basics and common Maay words / Aasaaska Af-Maay
knowledge.text:
Af-Maay (Maay Maay, Mai-Mai) is spoken by roughly 2.75 million people, mainly the Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn) and many Somali Bantu, in Bay, Bakool, Gedo, the Shabelle and Jubba regions (Baidoa/Baydhabo, Buurhakaba, Diinsoor, Afgooye area), and in parts of Ethiopia and Kenya. Dialects include Maay Erte, Maay Dhete and Af-Helledi.
How Maay differs from Standard (Maxaa) Somali (Hassan 2011, citing Saeed, Lehman & Eno, Tosco):
- No pharyngeal sounds: Maay lacks the c (ʕ) and x (ħ) of Maxaa (they appear only in loans).
- Extra sounds written p, jh, gh, ng, ny, and a final vowel often written -y: e.g., magh-y 'noun', misgy 'sorghum', jyny 'heaven' (examples from Maay writers). Maay writers use letters like d', y', g' for implosive sounds.
- Fewer or no preverbal focus particles (no waa / baa system as in Maxaa); different question determiner (ko/to vs Maxaa kee/tee). Word order is freer (SVO common).
- Many everyday words differ: sun = iry (Maxaa qorrax); fish = malalay (Maxaa kalluun).
Phrase comparisons from community sources (spellings vary; treat as approximate):
| Maay | Standard Somali | English |
| See eta? | Sidee tahay? | How are you? |
| Ani faylena | Waan fiicanahay | I'm fine |
| See ku bari'di? | Sidee ku baryay? | Good morning (how did you wake?) |
| Nebedgeliyo | Nabadgelyo | Goodbye |
| Sa dhowaaw | Soo dhawoow | Welcome |
| Mahadsinta | Mahadsanid | Thank you |
| Inka raali ahaaw | Iga raalli ahow | Excuse me |
| Ani / Adi / Usu / Iyi / Unu | Aniga / Adiga / Isaga / Iyada / Annaga | I / you / he / she / we |
| Eed | Aad | Very |
| May fathaasy? | Maxaa rabtaa? | What do you want? |
| Ki salaamye | Waan ku salaamay | I greet you |
| Famahteey? / Fahami / Mi fahamnih | Ma fahantay? / Waan fahmay / Ma fahmin | Do you understand? / I understand / I don't understand |
| Mi feylihi | Ma fiicni (I'm not well) | I don't feel well |
Shared words: haa (yes), maya (no), ama (or), iyo (and), laakiin (but), kaalmo (help).
Assistant guidance: if a user writes or speaks Maay, reply in clear Standard Somali (which most Maay speakers understand) unless asked otherwise, keep sentences short, and avoid Northern idioms; never correct Maay as 'wrong Somali'. Do not fabricate Maay vocabulary beyond verified lists.

knowledge.title: Somali in Djibouti, Ethiopia and Kenya / Af-Soomaaliga Jabuuti, Itoobiya iyo Kenya
knowledge.text:
Somali is spoken across the Horn of Africa, not only in Somalia and Somaliland.
Djibouti (Jabuuti): Somali (mainly Ciise/Issa and Gadabuursi speech of the Northern group) is a national language beside Afar; the official languages are French and Arabic. Expect French loanwords and code-switching in daily and administrative talk (e.g., currency "faran" from franc). Djiboutian Somali is close to Hargeysa speech.
Ethiopia: the Somali Region (Deegaanka Soomaalida, capital Jigjiga / Jijiga) uses Somali as its official working language in government and schools. Speech belongs mainly to the Northern Darod/Ogaden and Northern-proper groups; Amharic administrative terms and the currency birr appear in daily language. Major towns: Jigjiga, Godey (Gode), Qabridahare, Dhagaxbuur, Wardheer, Doolow.
Kenya: Somali is widely spoken in the former North Eastern Province (Garissa / Gaarisa, Wajir / Wajeer, Mandera / Mandheera) and in Nairobi's Eastleigh (Islii). Kenyan Somali mixes in Swahili and English words (e.g., money in Kenyan shillings, "matatu" minibuses, school terms in English) and some speakers use Garre or Borana as well. Many Kenyan Somalis write with English-influenced spelling (Abdi, Mohamed, Hassan) rather than official Somali spelling (Cabdi, Maxamed, Xasan).
Diaspora: large communities in the UK, USA (Minnesota, Ohio), Canada, Sweden, Norway, the Netherlands, Turkey, the UAE and South Africa. Young diaspora speakers code-switch heavily with English or the local language, use English spelling for names and slang, and sometimes drop the official letters c, x and dh in chat (writing "3" or "c"/"a" and "x"/"h" inconsistently).
For an assistant: identify location by context (currency, place names) rather than guessing from accent; accept loanwords from French, Amharic, Swahili and English as normal Somali usage in those communities; give prices in the right currency (Djiboutian franc, Ethiopian birr, Kenyan shilling, Somali/Somaliland shilling, US dollar).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_dialects; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Spelling variants and non-standard spellings / Kala duwanaanshaha higgaadda
knowledge.text:
The 1972 orthography is phonemic, but real-world Somali text shows systematic variation. A knowledge system should treat these pairs as the same word (normalise before searching or matching):
Dialect-based pairs
| xidh / xir (tie, close) | odhan / oran (to say) | idhi / iri, yidhi / yiri (said) | badh / bar (half) | adhi / ari (small livestock) |
| wakhti / waqti (time) | khudaar / qudaar (vegetables) | labo / laba (two) | todoba / toddoba (seven) | siddeed / sideed (eight) |
Vowel and ending variation
| -ay / -ey past endings: keenay / keeney, sameeyay / sameeyey | ay / ey inside words: samayn / sameyn, dawlad / dowlad (state) |
| aa vs a, ii vs i where length is unclear: raalli / raali (pleased), Ilaahay / Illaahay / Alle (God) |
| hooyaday / hooyadey (my mother), kayga / keyga (my) |
Doubled consonants change meaning, so do not 'simplify' them: amaan (safety, security) vs ammaan (praise), as in the proverb "Dumar nin ammaanaa leh" where ammaan = praise; write a double consonant only where the dictionary form has it.
Word division
- Compounds and particles are written joined or separate inconsistently: waxwalba / wax walba (everything), maxaa yeelay / maxaayeelay (because), Soomaaliland / Somaliland, iska warran / iskawarran. Standard practice is to write particles separately except fused clitics (waan, wuxuu, ii, kaaga).
- Hyphens appear in compounds: madax-xanuun / madaxxanuun (headache), cod-bixin / codbixin (voting).
Non-official (anglicised/Arabic/Italian-influenced) spellings
| Mohamed / Mohammed → Maxamed | Ali → Cali | Abdi → Cabdi | Hassan → Xasan | Hussein → Xuseen | Ahmed → Axmed | Omar → Cumar | Osman → Cusmaan | Fatima / Fadumo → Faadumo | Halima → Xaliimo | Hawa → Xaawo | Mogadishu → Muqdisho | Hargeisa → Hargeysa | Kismayo → Kismaayo | Galkayo → Gaalkacyo | Bosaso → Boosaaso | Beledweyne → Beledweyne / Baladweyne |
Chat spellings: diaspora users may write 3 for c (Ca3), 7 for x, or drop the letter entirely (Ali for Cali). Recognisers trained on other languages produce the anglicised forms by default.
Rule for the assistant: write Standard Somali with official letters (c, x, q, dh, kh, ') and long vowels, but accept every variant above in input. When quoting names, follow the person's own preferred spelling if known.
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/spec/orthography/0001-alphabet.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_alphabet; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar

knowledge.title: Technology and phone vocabulary / Erayada tignoolajiyada iyo taleefanka
knowledge.text:
Everyday tech words Somali speakers actually use (many are loans; spelling varies):
| taleefan / telefoon – telephone | moobayl / mobil – mobile phone | taleefanka gacanta – mobile phone (formal) |
| wicitaan – a call | wac – call! ("I soo wac" call me) | fariin / farriin – message, SMS | codad / cod – voice, voice note (also 'vote') |
| lambar / nambar – number | khad / khadka – line, connection | shabakad – network ("shabakaddu way xun tahay" the network is bad) |
| internet / internetka – internet | xog – data, information |
| kombiyuutar / kumbuyuutar – computer | laabtoob – laptop | shaashad – screen | kiiboodh – keyboard |
| barnaamij – program, app, broadcast programme | app / abka – app (loan) | websaydh / bogga internetka – website |
| sawir – photo, picture | muuqaal – video, image | maqal – audio |
| batari / beytari – battery | koronto / laydh (North) – electricity, power ("laydhkii waa go'ay" the power went off) |
| akoon / koonto – account | erayga sirta ah / furaha sirta – password | koodh – code (e.g., verification code) |
| emayl / iimayl – email | baraha bulshada – social media | xiriirka – contact(s) |
Action verbs (imperative form):
| dir – send | soo dir – send (to me) | fur – open, unlock | xir / xidh – close, turn off, lock | shid – turn on (a light, device) | dami – switch off, extinguish |
| raadi – search, look for | kaydi – save | tirtir – delete, erase | soo degso – download | geli / gal – enter, log in | ka bax – exit, log out |
| cusbooneysii – update | dib u bilow – restart | ku xir – connect ("Wi-Fi-ga ku xir") | qor – write, type | akhri – read | dhegeyso – listen |
Example sentences:
- "Fadlan code-ka la iigu soo diray ii sheeg" (Please tell me the code that was sent to me) – note: an assistant must never ask users to read out real verification codes to it unless the user is completing their own login.
- "Taleefankaygu wuu dansan yahay, batarigu wuu dhammaaday" (My phone is off, the battery died).
- "Abka cusbooneysii, kadibna dib u bilow" (Update the app, then restart).
- "Wi-Fi-ga furihiisu waa maxay?" (What's the Wi-Fi password?)
Brand and company names commonly spoken: Hormuud, Telesom, Golis, Somtel, Hormuud's EVC Plus, Telesom's ZAAD, Golis's Sahal, Somtel's eDahab, WhatsApp, TikTok, Facebook, YouTube.
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0)

knowledge.title: Health and medical vocabulary / Erayada caafimaadka
knowledge.text:
People and places:
| dhakhtar / dhakhtarad – doctor (m/f) | kalkaaliye / kalkaaliso – nurse (m/f) | umuliso – midwife | farmashiye / farmashiyaha – pharmacy |
| isbitaal – hospital | rug caafimaad / xarun caafimaad – clinic, health centre | shaybaar – laboratory | qolka gurmadka degdegga – emergency room |
| ambalaas – ambulance | bukaan – patient, sick person | daawo – medicine | kaniini – tablet, pill |
| irbad – injection, needle | talaal – vaccination | baaritaan – examination, test | raajo – X-ray |
| qalliin – surgery, operation | dhiig – blood | cadaadiska dhiigga – blood pressure | sonkorta – blood sugar |
Symptoms and conditions:
| xanuun – pain, illness | qandho – fever | qufac – cough | hargab – cold, flu | madax-xanuun – headache |
| calool-xanuun – stomach ache | shuban – diarrhoea | matag – vomiting | lallabo – nausea | wareer – dizziness |
| neef-qabatin – shortness of breath, asthma | duumo – malaria | sonkorow – diabetes | dhiig-kar – high blood pressure |
| kansar – cancer | jab – fracture | dhaawac – injury, wound | gubasho – burn | xasaasiyad – allergy |
| uur – pregnancy ("uur leh" pregnant) | dhalmo / umul – childbirth | nafaqo-darro – malnutrition | fuuq-bax – dehydration | walwal – anxiety, worry |
Useful sentences:
- "Maxaa ku xanuunaya?" (What hurts?) – "Madaxa ayaa i xanuunaya" (My head hurts). "Calooshaa i xanuunaysa" (My stomach hurts).
- "Qandho ayaan qabaa" (I have a fever). "Waan xanuunsanahay" (I'm ill). "Ma ka roonaatay?" (Are you better?)
- "Daawadan maalintii saddex jeer qaado" (Take this medicine three times a day). "Cuntada kadib" (after meals). "Ka hor cuntada" (before meals).
- "Ma leedahay xasaasiyad daawo?" (Do you have a medicine allergy?)
- "Ambalaas u yeer!" (Call an ambulance!) "Gargaar degdeg ah ayaan u baahanahay" (I need urgent help).
Assistant note: give general health information only, encourage seeing a dhakhtar for diagnosis, and treat emergencies ("dhiig badan", "neef la'aan", "miyir-beel" – fainting/unconsciousness) by urging immediate care.
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; https://www.omniglot.com/pdfs/somali_for_doctors.pdf

knowledge.title: School and education vocabulary / Erayada waxbarashada
knowledge.text:
| waxbarasho – education | barasho – learning | dugsi – school | iskuul – school (loan, common in speech) |
| dugsi Quraan / malcaamad – Qur'anic school | dugsiga hoose – primary school | dugsiga dhexe – intermediate school | dugsiga sare – secondary school |
| jaamacad – university | kulliyad – faculty, college | machad – institute | xanaano – nursery, kindergarten |
| macallin / macallimad – teacher (m/f); plural macallimiin | arday – student(s) | ardayad – female student | maamule – principal, director |
| fasal – class, classroom, grade ("fasalka saddexaad" third grade) | cashar – lesson | layli – exercise, homework | imtixaan – exam |
| natiijo – result | dhibco / buundo – marks, score | shahaado – certificate, diploma | qalin-jabin – graduation (lit. breaking the pen) |
| buug – book (plural buugaag) | qalin – pen, pencil (plural qalammo) | warqad – paper, letter | sabuurad – blackboard |
| maktabad – library | manhaj – curriculum | sannad-dugsiyeedka – school year | fasax – holiday, leave |
Subjects: xisaab (mathematics), saynis (science), fiisigis (physics), kimistari (chemistry), bayoolaji (biology), juqraafi (geography), taariikh (history), luqadda Soomaaliga / Af-Soomaali, Ingiriisi (English), Carabi (Arabic), tarbiyada Islaamka (Islamic education), tiknoolaji / ICT, ganacsi (business studies).
Useful sentences:
- "Fasalkee ayaad dhigataa?" (Which grade are you in?) – "Fasalka toddobaad" (seventh grade).
- "Imtixaanka goorma ayuu bilaabmayaa?" (When does the exam start?)
- "Layliga guriga ma dhammeysay?" (Did you finish your homework?)
- "Waxaan dhigtaa jaamacadda, kulliyadda caafimaadka" (I study at university, in the faculty of medicine).
- "Natiijada imtixaanka shahaadiga ah" (the national certificate exam result).
Note: "dhig" means both 'put down' and 'study/teach' (dhigo = study, "wax dhig" = teach). "Qalin-jabin" ceremonies are major family events; congratulate with "Hambalyo, qalin-jabin wanaagsan!"
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. knowledge.title: Loanwords in modern Somali: Arabic, Italian, English / Ereyada ka soo galay luqadaha kale
knowledge.text:
Somali has absorbed many words through Islam, trade and colonial rule. Knowing the origin helps recognition and spelling.
From Arabic (largest group; religion, law, education, abstract ideas, many daily words):
macallin (teacher, from muʻallim), qalin (pen, from qalam), kitaab (book, esp. religious), maktabad (library), sharci (law), dowlad (state), wakhti / waqti (time), saacad (hour, clock, watch), salaad (prayer), Ramadaan, sako (zakat), sadaqo (charity), khayr (good), shar (evil), sabab (reason), xaq (right, truth), xaalad (situation), kursi (chair), qaamuus (dictionary), jaamacad (university), shahaado (certificate), sayid, sheekh, duco (prayer), iimaan (faith), samir (patience).
From Italian (mostly southern Somalia, cars, food, offices):
baabuur (motor vehicle – Arabic bābūr, ultimately Italian vapore 'steam'), baasto (pasta), shukumaan (towel, from asciugamano), fasoolya (beans, fagioli), koronto (electricity, from corrente).
From English (mostly northern Somalia; technology, medicine, education):
buug (book), iskuul (school), isbitaal (hospital), dhakhtar (doctor), taleefan (telephone), kombiyuutar (computer), baasaboor (passport), booliis (police), tigidh (ticket), bas (bus), tagsi (taxi), kiilo (kilo), batari (battery), internet, emayl, laabtoob (laptop).
From other languages: bajaaj (Indian brand name → three-wheeled taxi), rooti (bread, via Hindi/Arabic), shaah (tea, Persian/Arabic chai/shay), faran (Djibouti franc, French), birr (Ethiopian currency, Amharic).
Adaptation rules visible in loans: Somali has no p or v, so they become b or f (pasta → baasto, vapore → baabuur, police → booliis); consonant clusters get extra vowels (school → iskuul, ticket → tigidh); final vowels added (bus → bas, kilo → kiilo). Terminology projects (e.g., the Somali Language Standard and the Somali language academies) also coin native Somali terms for new concepts; prefer an established term when one exists.
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/tree/main/data/lexicon (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Hassan, Deqa (2011). Somali Dialects in the United States: How Intelligible is Af-Maay to Speakers of Af-Maxaa? MA thesis, Minnesota State Univ. https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/etds/276/

knowledge.title: The Somali Latin alphabet and its special letters / Alifbeetada Af-Soomaaliga
knowledge.text:
The official Somali script (Far Soomaali / Farta Laatiinka) was adopted on 21 October 1972. Letter order:
B T J X KH D R S SH DH C G F Q K L M N W H Y, plus the vowels A E I O U and the glottal stop written with an apostrophe (').
Letters whose values differ from English (the main source of mispronunciation and mistranscription):
| C c – voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], the Arabic ʿayn (ع). Cali (Ali), Cumar (Omar), caano (milk), Carabi (Arabic). Never pronounced like English 'c'/'k'. |
| X x – voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the Arabic ḥā' (ح): a strong breathy h from the throat. Xasan (Hassan), Xamar, xalay (last night), xoolo (livestock). Never 'ks'. |
| Q q – uvular stop, often voiced [ɢ] or [q], deep in the throat: qalin (pen), Qur'aan, suuq (market), Muqdisho. |
| DH dh – voiced retroflex stop [ɖ], tongue curled back; between vowels it often sounds like a flapped r [ɽ]: dhul (land), gabadha (the girl), odhan. |
| KH kh – velar/uvular fricative [χ] like Arabic خ, mostly in Arabic loans: khamiis (Thursday), khayr (good), wakhti (time). |
| ' – glottal stop [ʔ]: ra'iis (president/chief), lo' (cattle), su'aal (question), ba'an (severe). |
| SH sh = English 'sh'; J j = English 'j' (jaamacad); G g is always hard ('go'), never 'j'; H h is a plain h; Y and W as in English. |
Somali has no native p, v or z (loans adapt them: pasta → baasto, police → booliis) and no 'ch' sound in native words.
Vowels: a e i o u, each short or long (doubled): aa ee ii oo uu. Length changes meaning (see the vowel-length entry). Each vowel also has a 'front' and 'back' (tongue-root) quality that is not written. Diphthongs: ay/ey (as in 'my'/'may'), aw/ow (as in 'cow'/'go'), oy: "maya", "dowlad", "hooyo".
Writing conventions: one letter = one sound, so spelling is phonetic. Doubled consonants are pronounced longer/stronger (dd, gg, ll, mm, nn, bb, rr): "aabbe", "hooyada", "ammaan". Capitalise names and sentence starts as in English; names of days/months are capitalised in standard usage (Isniin, Maarso). Arabic religious phrases are written in Somali spelling: "Insha Allah" or "Haddii Alle idmo", "Alxamdulillaah", "Bismillaahi".
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/spec/orthography/0001-alphabet.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_alphabet; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_phonology; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Vowel length, double consonants, tone and stress / Dhererka shaqallada, shibbanayaasha labanlaaban iyo codka
knowledge.text:
Vowel length is phonemic – a single short vs long vowel makes a different word. Minimal pairs:
| bur (flour) – buur (mountain) | dar (put, add) – daar (building) | gal (enter) – gaal (non-Muslim, foreigner) |
| tag (go) – taag (stand up; strength) | dib (back, again) – diib (hand over) | did (faint) – diid (refuse) |
A recogniser or TTS that ignores length will confuse these. Write long vowels doubled; never use accents for length.
Double (geminate) consonants also distinguish words and are pronounced with more force: amaan (safety) – ammaan (praise). The k/t article creates many geminates: buug → buugga, bad → badda, nin → ninka (no geminate), ilma → ilmaha.
Tone/accent (not written): Somali has a pitch accent – one high-pitched mora in the last or second-to-last position of a word. It marks:
- gender: ínan 'boy' vs inán 'girl'; many masculine nouns stress the penultimate, feminine nouns the final mora;
- case: the name Faadumo has different accent patterns as subject, object, possessor and vocative (Faadúmo, Faadumo, Faadumó, Fàadumo – Saeed);
- singular vs plural in some nouns, and question intonation.
For TTS: keep the default stress near the end of the word and slightly raise the last syllable of yes/no questions. For ASR: tone is lost in writing, so disambiguate gender/number from context (verb agreement, articles).
Other phonetic notes:
- Between vowels, b, d, g are softened (approximants/fricatives): "aabbe" keeps a full b because it is doubled; "magac" has a soft g.
- dh between vowels sounds close to a flapped r, which is why Northern dh and Southern r alternate (xidh/xir).
- Glottal stop and pharyngeals (c, x) can be weak in fast or diaspora speech: "Cali" may sound like "Ali", "Xasan" like "Hasan". Normalise to the standard spelling in transcripts.
- Maay lacks c and x entirely and has extra sounds (p, jh, gh, ng, ny), so a Maay speaker's "Ali" is genuinely Ali.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_phonology; Hassan, Deqa (2011). Somali Dialects in the United States: How Intelligible is Af-Maay to Speakers of Af-Maxaa? MA thesis, Minnesota State Univ. https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/etds/276/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maay_language; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Speech recognition guide: Somali words often mistranscribed / Hagaha aqoonsiga codka
knowledge.text:
General-purpose speech recognisers often mistake Somali for Spanish, Italian, Hindi/Urdu, Arabic or Swahili because Somali shares their open vowels and many sounds, and they output those languages' spellings. Typical systematic errors and the correct Somali spelling:
- Pharyngeal c dropped or written as 'a/e': Cali (not Ali), Cabdi (not Abdi), Cumar (not Omar), Caasha (not Aisha), caano (milk), cunto (food), cusub (new), ciyaar (game, play), Ciid (Eid).
- Pharyngeal x written as h/j/kh: Xasan (not Hassan/Jasan), Xamar, xalay, xaafad (neighbourhood), xanuun (pain), xoolo, Xaliimo, Xamse.
- q written as k/g: qalin, qof (person), qoys (family), qiime (price), Muqdisho, suuq, Qur'aan.
- dh written as d/r: dhakhtar (doctor), dhul, dhammaan (all), dhaqan (culture), Dhuusamareeb.
- Long vowels shortened (meaning changes): waan (I – focus) vs wan (ram); buur (mountain) vs bur (flour); taag vs tag.
- Short high-frequency words are easily dropped or merged: "haa" (yes), "waa", "iyo" (and), "oo", "ma" (question/negation) – check that they survive in the transcript.
- Clitic clusters split wrongly: "iigu soo dir" (send it to me) should not become "ii gu so dir"; "wuxuu" not "wu xuu"; "ma'aha" → "ma aha".
Very common words to bias recognition toward (sample; the full list is in the ASR vocabulary file):
Function words: waa, waan, waad, wuu, way, baa, ayaa, waxaan, waxaad, wuxuu, waxay, ma, maya, haa, haye, iyo, oo, ee, laakiin, haddii, markaas, sidoo kale, maxaa, xaggee, immisa, goorma, sidee, yaa. Religious: Alxamdulillaah, Insha Allah, Maasha Allah, Bismillaahi, Subxaanallaah, Ilaahay, Ilaahay ha u naxariisto, salaad, masjid, Ramadaan, Ciid. Places: Muqdisho, Hargeysa, Kismaayo, Garoowe, Boosaaso, Baydhabo, Beledweyne, Gaalkacyo, Burco, Berbera, Boorama, Laascaanood, Ceerigaabo, Jowhar, Marka, Afgooye, Dhuusamareeb, Baraawe, Jigjiga, Jabuuti, Nayroobi, Soomaaliya, Soomaaliland, Puntland. Brands/services: Hormuud, EVC Plus, Telesom, ZAAD, Golis, Sahal, Somtel, eDahab, Dahabshiil, Salaam Bank, Premier Bank. Rule for a Somali-first assistant: run Somali as the forced recognition language when the user's profile says Somali, add this vocabulary as a bias/hint list, and post-correct transcripts by restoring c/x/q/dh and long vowels in known words. If a transcript contains Spanish- or Italian-looking text in a Somali conversation, assume misrecognition rather than a language switch.

knowledge.title: Somali naming customs: patronymic names and genealogy / Magac-bixinta Soomaalida
knowledge.text:
Somalis do not use inherited family surnames. A full name is a patronymic chain:
given name + father's given name + paternal grandfather's given name (and further ancestors if needed). Example: Cali Maxamed Xasan = Cali, son of Maxamed, son of Xasan. His daughter would be Faadumo Cali Maxamed. Siblings share the second and third names; cousins share only the third.
Consequences an assistant must handle:
- The 'last name' on a passport or form is usually the grandfather's name, not a family name; brothers and sisters have the same 'surname' but their children's change.
- Women keep their own patronymic names after marriage; a wife does not take her husband's name. "Mrs. Cali" is not a Somali usage.
- Common forms of address: given name alone, given name + father's name, or given name + nickname (naanays). Elders and officials are often called by title + name (Sheekh Cabdi, Dr. Faadumo, Madaxweyne Xasan).
- Diaspora documents sometimes record names in a different order or with English spelling (Mohamed Ali Hassan); match records on all name parts, not just the last one.
- "Ina" means 'son of' in poetic/common reference: Ina Cabdille Xasan (the poet-leader Sayid Maxamed Cabdille Xasan).
Genealogy (abtirsiin): reciting one's male-line ancestry is a traditional way to place a person socially; "Isir" means descent/origin, "tol" kin, "qabiil" clan. Asking a stranger's clan can be sensitive; an assistant should not ask about or infer clan from a name.
Naming a baby (magac-bixin): babies usually receive an Islamic or Somali name within the first week, often with an aqiiqo (sacrifice/celebration). First sons are frequently named Maxamed and first daughters Faadumo in many families; names honouring grandparents are common. Day-names exist too, e.g., Axado for a girl born on Sunday (Axad), noted by Kapchits.
Spelling: official Somali spelling uses c, x, q, dh (Cabdullaahi, Xaliimo, Maxamed); international documents usually use English or Italian transliteration (Abdullahi, Halima, Mohamed / Mohammed / Mohamud). Both refer to the same names.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_people

knowledge.title: Nicknames (naanays) and short forms / Naanaysyada
knowledge.text:
Naanays (nickname) culture is strong in Somali society: because many people share the same given names (Maxamed, Cali, Faadumo...), a descriptive nickname distinguishes them and often becomes part of the public name, even in politics and the media. Nicknames can be affectionate, humorous or blunt, and are usually based on appearance, character, origin or an anecdote.
Common descriptive naanays (with meaning):
| Dheere – the tall one | Gaab / Gaabow – the short one | Yare – the little/young one | Weyne – the big one |
| Cadde – the light-skinned one | Madoobe – the dark one | Gacmadheere – long-armed (generous) | Afweyne – big mouth |
| Indhacasse – red-eyed | Bidix – left-handed | Laangadh – limping | Timacadde – white-haired |
| Qoorweyne – thick-necked | Faruur – thick-lipped |
Famous examples: Maxamed Siyaad Barre was widely called "Afweyne" ('big mouth'); many public figures are better known by their naanays than by their patronymic chain.
Affectionate and short forms: the many Cabd- names are often shortened to Cabdi in speech; names ending in -o/-e may take the vocative: "Faadumeey!", "Calow!", "Xaliimooy!" Children and elders may be called "Aabbo", "Hooyo", "Abti", "Adeer", "Ayeeyo" instead of names.
Etiquette for an assistant: use a nickname only if the user introduces themselves with it or asks to be called by it; some naanays (about disability, skin colour or weight) are rude when used by outsiders. When a user says "Waxaa la i yiraahdaa Dheere" (I'm called Dheere), store it as the preferred name. When searching contacts, match both the nickname and the formal name ("Cali Dheere" = Cali Maxamed Xasan).
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siad_Barre

knowledge.title: Common mistakes machines make in Somali (and fixes) / Khaladaadka caadiga ah
knowledge.text:
Checklist for an AI writing or speaking Somali:
1. Gender agreement by grammar, not by natural sex or English: feminine subject → -t- verb form. "Asli baa keentay" (not *keenay). "Deeradu biyo bay cabtay" (deero is feminine). Countries and cities are feminine: "Soomaaliya way horumartay". 2. Missing subject clitic after an object focus: "Wiilkii moos buu cunay" (not *moos baa cunay); "Adigu moos baad cuntay" (not *baa cuntay). 3. Two focus markers in one main clause, or none in a declarative: say "Waan imanayaa" or "Berri baan imanayaa", not *"Berri baan waan imanayaa" or a bare "Aniga imanayaa". 4. Doubled ma in negative questions: "Axmed miyaanu imanayn?" or "Ma Axmed baan iman?", not *"Axmed ma ma imanayo?". 5. Regularising irregular verbs: imow → yimid/timid/imid (not *imoway); dheh → yiri/tiri/iri; ahaan → ahaa/ahayd. 6. Treating progressive and simple past as the same: "cunay" (ate) ≠ "cunayay" (was eating). 7. Omitting required prepositions: "Kursiga ku fariiso" (sit ON the chair), "Ka bax" (go out FROM), "U baahan" (need FOR): *"Kursiga fariiso" sounds wrong. 8. Plural nouns after numbers: "laba buug", "saddex sano", not *"laba buugag". 9. English word order and calques: "Waxaan rabaa inaan tago" (I want to go) – not *"Aniga rabaa tag". Avoid literal idioms ("sorry for your loss" → use "Ilaahay ha u naxariisto"). 10. Missing linker in multi-modifier phrases: "dukaanka dharka ee Cali" (Ali's clothes shop). 11. Dropping c, x, q, dh or long vowels: Cali, Xasan, qof, dhakhtar, waan/wan, buur/bur – these are different words. 12. Reduced agreement is NOT an error with a focused plural subject: "Nimankii baa yimid" is correct. 13. Mixing dialect spellings inside one text (xidh and xir, wakhti and waqti) – pick one. 14. Over-formal or Arabic-heavy wording for casual users; prefer everyday words (e.g., shaqo 'work', caawimaad 'help', lacag 'money'). 15. Inventing proverbs, Maay words or names. If unsure, say so or use plain language. SLS guidance: a checker should report 'not covered' rather than 'error' when a construction is outside reviewed rules, and should name the rule violated instead of silently rewriting the user's text.
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/spec/grammar/0017-common-mistakes.md (CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Core assistant phrases in Somali (service and help) / Erayada caawinaadda
knowledge.text:
Phrases a Somali-first assistant (chat, bots, live voice) uses constantly – natural, polite Standard Somali:
Opening and offering help:
- "Assalaamu calaykum! Sideen kuu caawin karaa?" (Hello! How can I help you?)
- "Maxaan kuu qabtaa maanta?" (What can I do for you today?)
- "Haa, waan ku caawin karaa." (Yes, I can help you.) "Hadda ayaan eegayaa." (I'm checking now.)
Clarifying:
- "Ma ii sharxi kartaa wax yar?" (Can you explain a little more?)
- "Ma waxaad ula jeeddaa ...?" (Do you mean ...?) "Ma sidaas baa?" (Is that right?)
- "Fadlan ku celi, si fiican kuuma maqlin." (Please repeat, I didn't hear you well.)
- "Magaca sidee loo qoraa?" (How is the name spelled?) "Lambarka mar kale ii sheeg." (Tell me the number again.)
Confirming and acting:
- "Waa hagaag, waan sameeyay." (OK, I've done it.) "Waa la diray." (It has been sent.)
- "Ma hubtaa inaad rabto inaan diro?" (Are you sure you want me to send it?) "Ma xaqiijinaysaa?" (Do you confirm?)
- "Daqiiqad i sug." (Wait a moment.) "Wax yar ayay qaadan doontaa." (It will take a little while.)
When unable:
- "Waan ka xumahay, taas ma samayn karo." (Sorry, I can't do that.)
- "Macluumaad ku filan ma hayo." (I don't have enough information.) "Ma hubo." (I'm not sure.)
- "Waxaad u baahan kartaa inaad la xiriirto ..." (You may need to contact ...)
Closing:
- "Ma jiraa wax kale oo aan kuu qabto?" (Is there anything else I can do for you?)
- "Mahadsanid, maalin wanaagsan!" / "Nabadgelyo, Ilaahay kuu fududeeyo." (Thanks, have a good day! / Goodbye, may God make it easy for you.)
Style rules: use "adiga/aad" (singular you) for one user; "idinka/aad ... -teen" only for groups. Keep sentences short for voice. Prefer "Waan ku caawin karaa" over literal English constructions. Use the user's name or "walaal". Mirror the user's dialect spellings when echoing names and places, but keep Standard Somali grammar.
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0)

knowledge.title: Islam in Somalia (Diinta Islaamka ee Soomaaliya): overview
knowledge.text:
Islam is the religion of almost all Somalis in Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and North Eastern Kenya, and it is woven into daily speech, law, family life and identity. The Provisional Constitution of the Federal Republic of Somalia (2012) names Islam as the state religion and says no law may contradict the general principles of Sharia; Somaliland's constitution says the same for its territory.

Islam reached the Somali coast very early, through Arabian and Persian traders and through the ports of Zeila (Saylac), Berbera, Mogadishu (Muqdisho), Marka and Baraawe. Somali tradition holds that the Masjid al-Qiblatayn in Zeila is one of the oldest mosques in Africa, and Mogadishu's Fakr ad-Din mosque dates from the 13th century. Medieval Muslim states such as the Sultanate of Ifat, the Adal Sultanate and the Ajuran Sultanate made the region part of the wider Islamic world.

Somalis are overwhelmingly Sunni Muslims and follow the Shafi'i school (madhhab) of jurisprudence, in common with Yemen, the East African Swahili coast and Southeast Asia. In theology most follow the Ash'ari tradition. Sufi brotherhoods (dariiqo, from Arabic tariqa) have shaped Somali religious life for centuries, especially the Qaadiriya, the Axmadiya and its offshoot the Saalixiya. From the 1970s onward, reformist (Salafi-leaning) movements spread, partly through study and work in the Gulf, and today Somali religious life ranges from traditional Sufi practice to reformist currents. The assistant should treat all mainstream Somali Muslim practice respectfully and not take sides in disputes between them.

Religious learning starts young: children attend dugsi (Qur'an school), where a macallin teaches them to read and memorise the Qur'an using the wooden board (loox). A person who has memorised the whole Qur'an is a xaafid. Religious scholars are called sheekh or culimo (plural, ulama), and many towns have a respected local sheikh who leads prayers, gives fatwas on daily issues and officiates marriages.

Religious terms are part of everyday Somali: Insha Allah (God willing), Alxamdulillaah (praise be to God), Mashaa Allah (what God has willed, said in admiration), Bismillaah (in the name of God, said before eating, starting work or travelling). Non-Muslim Somalis exist but are a very small minority; there is a small, historically present Christian community. Religious conversion away from Islam is a highly sensitive subject.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufism_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Qiblatayn_(Zeila)

knowledge.title: Sufi orders in Somalia (Dariiqooyinka Suufiyada): Qaadiriya, Axmadiya, Saalixiya
knowledge.text:
Sufism (tasawwuf) has been a central part of Somali Islam since at least the medieval period, and from the 19th century three brotherhoods (dariiqo, plural dariiqooyin) dominated: the Qaadiriya, the Axmadiya and the Saalixiya.

Qaadiriya (Qadiriyya): the oldest and most widespread order, tracing its chain to Sheikh Abdul Qadir al-Jilani of Baghdad (12th century). In Somalia it split into branches such as the Uwaysiya, founded by Sheikh Uways al-Barawi (Shiikh Uweys, 1847–1909) of Baraawe, who wrote religious poetry in Somali (Maay) and Arabic, and the Zayla'iya branch associated with Sheikh Abdirahman al-Zayla'i (Shiikh Cabdiraxmaan Seylici) in the north. Sheikh Uways was killed in 1909 by followers of the rival Saalixiya, a well-known episode in Somali religious history.

Axmadiya (Ahmadiyya, also Idrisiyya): derived from the teachings of Ahmad ibn Idris al-Fasi (died 1837), spread in southern Somalia especially along the Shabeelle river, where its followers founded agricultural religious settlements (jamaaco).

Saalixiya (Salihiyya): a branch founded by Muhammad Salih in Mecca; it became famous in Somalia because Sayid Maxamed Cabdulle Xasan, leader of the Dervish movement (1899–1920), belonged to it and used it to mobilise resistance against British, Italian and Ethiopian forces.

Characteristic Sufi practices include dhikr (Somali: dikri or xadra), collective chanting of God's names and religious poems; the celebration of Mawlid (Mawliid) for the Prophet's birthday; reciting qasidas and the Burda; and siyaaro, annual visits to the tombs of saints (awliyo), such as the tomb of Sheikh Uways at Biyooley or of Sheikh Isaaq at Maydh. Settled religious communities called jamaaco historically offered refuge, farming land and education.

Since the 1970s, reformist movements have criticised practices like saint veneration and siyaaro as innovations, and debates continue. During the civil war, the Sufi-identified militia Ahlu Sunna Wal Jamaaca (formed 2008) fought al-Shabaab, partly in response to its destruction of Sufi shrines. When users ask, the assistant should describe Sufi traditions factually and respectfully, without declaring any practice right or wrong; for rulings, suggest consulting a trusted local scholar.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufism_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uways_al-Barawi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qadiriyya; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahlu_Sunna_Waljama%27a
